title: Aftercare Program Supports Long-Term Recovery in California
summary: At CoreCivic's Boston Avenue reentry facility former residents can engage in Aftercare, a group established to help individuals maintain their recovery by providing a supportive, judgement-free environment where they can continue to learn, grow and stay connected to their recovery community.
body_markdown:
For many justice-involved individuals navigating reentry, the need for support and tools for success extends beyond their time in a facility or community reentry center. Rehabilitation and recovery are ongoing processes that require commitment, connection and support.


At CoreCivic’s **Boston Avenue** male community reentry program (MCRP) in San Diego, former residents and participants can now engage in Aftercare, a group established to help individuals maintain their recovery after completing treatment by providing a supportive, judgment-free environment where they can continue to learn, grow and stay connected to their recovery community.


The Aftercare group was established in 2025 by Boston Avenue treatment counselor Alice Beans, who said she recognized a need for additional resources for participants as they transition back into their daily lives. Many face challenges with employment, housing and reconnecting with their families, all while trying to maintain their sobriety. Aftercare provides a space where they can discuss these challenges and, through the guidance of those who have been in their shoes, develop strategies to overcome these obstacles.


“They talk about their challenges and remaining accountable for their recovery,” Beans said. “They appreciate being able to have a safe and judgment-free zone where they can share if they’re struggling or doing well.”


Aftercare participants meet in public spaces and engage in group discussions focused on practical topics to help each individual maintain recovery and improve overall well-being. Topics include stress management, relapse prevention, communication skills, healthy decision-making and more.


“For me, Aftercare is knowing that even though the MCRP program may be over, the support isn’t,” said Mr. Payne, a Boston Avenue graduate. “I still have people in my corner, and that means a lot to me.


“For me, Aftercare is about maintaining continuity in my treatment and recovery. It means continuing the relationships I’ve built with like-minded men who understand where I’ve been and are walking through similar stages in their own recovery.”


The Aftercare group also celebrates milestones and achievements together, such as a participant reaching a sobriety anniversary, landing a job, finding stable housing or achieving a personal goal. Celebrating successes helps reinforce positive behavior and motivates participants to keep moving forward.


“Being part of Aftercare has been really important to me,” said Mr. McDowell, a Boston Avenue graduate. “Finishing the MCRP program doesn’t mean everything suddenly becomes easy. Having a place to come back to, stay connected and talk with people who understand what you’re going through has made a big difference. Aftercare gives me accountability, but it also gives me a sense of belonging.”


Several Aftercare participants say staying engaged in the group has helped boost their confidence and commitment to recovery. Continued support and regular participation help them stay focused on their goals while reducing feelings of isolation.


Beans said the Aftercare group is committed to creating a positive, respectful and supportive atmosphere where participants can continue to build healthy lifestyles. Through peer connection, accountability and ongoing encouragement, the group helps individuals develop the skills and support systems necessary for lasting recovery and successful reintegration into the community.


“To me, Aftercare is a reminder that we don’t have to walk the next chapter alone,” Payne said. “We have people beside us who understand the journey, believe in our recovery and are willing to help us keep moving forward.”
